title: I’ve been working on an MNQ system for the last few months and I finally got to the point where started trying to break the whole thing.
author: eribertito

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the thing I'd check first is how each day gets its volatility bucket. if low/medium/high is decided using anything from that day's own session, the mean reversion legs are quietly peeking, and that tends to show up exactly as a smooth combined curve.

also worth knowing whether the four were picked before June 2020 or after seeing it. a shared OOS window chosen after the fact isn't really out of sample for the portfolio, even if it is for each piece.

replies.author: eribertito
replies.body:
Yeah, that's a fair point. The way I phrased the OOS in the post makes it sound like I just picked a bunch of strategies and then decided that everything after 2020 was OOS.
What I actually did was test each strategy independently using rolling development and out-of-sample periods. I used roughly 6 months of development and then 3 months of out of sample, with multiple windows spread across the dataset. The strategies were tested on periods both before and after 2020, so the final portfolio wasn't built just by looking at the post-2020 data.
For the volatility buckets, those were also based on the information available at the time of each trade, not the completed session. So there wasn't any lookahead from using the day's final volatility to classify the trades.
I probably should've explained the validation process better in the post, so I appreciate you pointing it out

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: rolling dev and OOS per strategy is a lot more convincing than how the post read. that's basically walk-forward, and it answers most of what I was poking at.
